doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Benny Carter, Bob Thiele's Basie request, and Danny Kaye date
summary: Carter backs Katz's own solo over the producer's Basie request, and Katz refuses a Basie cliche on a Warner date.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: something. It was very nice. We did it in two days, a lot of musicians there, and Benny Carter’s music plays itself. But now this is a class man, this Benny Carter. Because listen to what he did. On one of the tunes I had the bridge to play a little solo. Just eight bars I think. And I played it. I don’t remember which tune, it was probably “Honeysuckle Rose.” So when I did it Bob Thiele from the control room, after we did the take he says, “Uh Dick, can we have a little Count Basie in that spot?” Benny Carter took the microphone and says, “Bob if you don’t mind I’d like to hear a little Dick Katz in that place.” Now that was, to me, historic, because the overwhelming majority of the times, white or black, they want to please, whatever the guy said, do it. Do what he says.

Do what the producer says. Very often. They don’t want any trouble. It didn’t make that much difference for something like that. You know Tyree Glen would have said play Count Basie. The one time I rebelled at the end of a Warner — Danny Kaye had a terrific arrangement, I forget which tune, it might have been “Sandman” or something, and they had that [scats Basie ending] and I refused to play it. I played the rhythm but I changed the voicing. I just couldn’t bring myself to do it. Because even then it was like the cliché of all time.
I guess. And it always will be.
Yeah. So okay, where are we?
